142.0.s.en: (1) A cry to escape from the snare

142.0.0.en: I cried unto the LORD with my voice; with my voice unto the LORD did I make my supplication. I poured out my complaint before him; I shewed before him my trouble.

142.0.1.en: 1- David shows the extent of his suffering by four verbs: I cried, I made supplication, I poured out, and I shewed; in every way he shows his pains. The cry is from the depth of the heart. Supplication means humility, need and persistence. The pouring out shows the bringing forth of all that is within him, and this is evidence of his purity and his repentance from all evil. The showing means declaring his trouble in all its aspects, for he loves God, trusts in Him, and has the boldness of sonship, so he speaks with God with all his feelings.

142.0.2.en: 2- The variety of David's prayer with God shows his persistence in prayer at all times and in every form. And it shows that God is his only refuge, and consequently his attachment to God, and by this he obtains peace, even in the midst of severe trouble.

142.1.0.en: When my spirit was overwhelmed within me, then thou knewest my path. In the way wherein I walked have they privily laid a snare for me.

142.1.2.en: 1- David was greatly wearied by the weight of the trouble upon him, that is, his spirit was wearied within him. But he continued walking in virtue and righteousness, although the wicked laid a snare for him to make him fall, so that he would be hindered from righteousness and go away from God. But the trouble led him to fervent prayer and crying out to God. This shows David's love for God, for he did not murmur or show any evil in his heart.

142.1.3.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane, with His sweat falling like drops of blood, as He declared to the Father the weight of the sufferings and asked that the cup of suffering pass from Him (Lk 22:44), yet at the same time He was submissive to the divine will, which was the accomplishment of redemption. In His humanity He suffers pains, but He is submissive to the divinity within Him, and He still walked in righteousness although Satan rose up against Him and the Jews tried to ensnare Him with a word, and even to kill Him.

142.2.0.en: I looked on my right hand, and beheld, but there was no man that would know me: refuge failed me; no man cared for my soul.

142.2.2.en: 1- When the trouble increased upon David he looked on his right hand, that is, to his friends, servants, followers and loved ones, and found no one to help him, for all were occupied with other things than him, and he found no one to take refuge in and lean on.

142.2.3.en: All acted as though they did not know him, and consequently he found no one to ask about him or care to bring him out of the trouble, and there remained only God, to whom he lifted his eyes toward heaven, and he cried out and made supplication to Him.

142.2.4.en: 2- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, from whom all His loved ones were scattered, even His disciples closest to Him, who slept and left Him to pray alone in the Garden, and fled when He was arrested, and no one supported Him in His trials, torture and crucifixion because of their weakness.

142.2.5.en: Hasten to God in every trouble, for He feels for you and loves you and is able to deliver you, and if God wills He will direct people to help you, and by this you live steadily and are not disturbed by anything that passes over you.

142.3.0.en: I cried unto thee, O LORD: I said, Thou art my refuge and my portion in the land of the living.

142.3.1.en: 1- When people left David alone he found before him only God, so he cried out a second time and took refuge in Him, and found in Him the impregnable fortress that protects him with complete protection, even if he is alone and without a weapon or any earthly power.

142.3.2.en: 2- David also discovered that the Lord alone is his portion after people left him, and He is his portion in the land of the living, that is, throughout his life and not only at the time of trouble, so he enjoyed fellowship with God and became peaceful and joyful despite the trouble. And he believed that the Lord would remain his portion in the coming land of the living, that is, eternal life, where there is the complete enjoyment of being with God.

142.4.0.en: Attend unto my cry; for I am brought very low: deliver me from my persecutors; for they are stronger than I.

142.4.1.en: 1- David is still declaring his suffering to God, mentioning for the third time the word cry, and he begs God to take notice and attend to his cry, his plea being that he has been brought very low, that is, wearied greatly by the weight of the trouble upon him, but the useful thing is that he was brought low, that is, he humbled himself and clung to God, who has no helper but Him.

142.4.2.en: 2- The second reason for which David asks for God's swift intervention is that those who persecute him are stronger and mightier than he, for they are the rulers of the world and have great power; Saul is the king, and with him is the whole army, but God is of course stronger than Saul and any other power, and this shows David's faith in God.

142.5.0.en: Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name: the righteous shall compass me about; for thou shalt deal bountifully with me.

142.5.2.en: 1- David finally asks God to bring him out of prison, that is, the trouble he is passing through, which is the pursuit of Saul, who wants to kill him. By the prison he also means the psychological distress he suffers as a result of the evil of Saul and those with him, in addition to the scattering of David's loved ones from him, so he asks for rest for his soul, so that he may continue to be occupied with his goal, which is praising God and thanking Him, since he sees no goal for his life except the love of God and the enjoyment of praising Him.

142.5.3.en: 2- David also longs for his soul to be released from his body to rise to heaven and to live in continual praise to God in the Kingdom, where the saints surround him and praise God with him.

142.5.4.en: 3- David sees with the eye of hope that God has delivered him from his trouble, so the righteous were confirmed in their faith, and surrounded him to rejoice with him at God's bountiful dealing with him. Thus he returns with all the believers to the worship of God before the house of the Lord, that is, the tabernacle of meeting.

142.5.5.en: May you thank God when He delivers you from any trouble or gives you a new gift, for this is the feeling of a son with his father, so that you rejoice and also gladden the heart of God.

142.5.6.en: God saves those who please Him "Hear my prayer, O LORD, give ear to my supplications: in thy faithfulness answer me" v. 1 Introduction:

142.5.7.en: 1- Its author: the prophet David, as appears from the title of the psalm.

142.5.8.en: 2- When was it written? The title of this psalm in the Septuagint translation says that it is "of David, when his son was pursuing him," meaning Absalom.

142.5.9.en: 3- This psalm is similar to the psalm before it, but the preceding psalm focuses on the leaving of David by his loved ones, while this psalm focuses on the evil of the enemies who surround him.

142.5.10.en: 4- This psalm is the last of the seven penitential psalms, which are (Ps 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143). In this psalm there appears the joy of repentance and preparation for eternity, in addition to the remembrance of God's kindnesses, which stand over against man's sins.

142.5.11.en: 5- This psalm suits every believer who passes through trouble and hastens to repentance, and obtains God's mercies, which strengthen his hope in eternal life.

142.5.12.en: 6- This psalm is considered one of the Messianic psalms, because it speaks of the feelings of Christ as He approached the Cross and the darkness of the tomb.

142.5.13.en: 7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Prime, in which a person at the beginning of the day asks for God's help, remembers His kindnesses, and offers repentance for all his sins.

143.0.s.en: (1) A cry for deliverance from enemies

143.0.0.en: Hear my prayer, O LORD, give ear to my supplications: in thy faithfulness answer me, and in thy righteousness. And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified.

143.0.1.en: 1- We note that the beginning of this psalm is like the beginning of the preceding psalm, where David lifts his prayers and supplications to God because he is in trouble and his enemies have risen against him, although he did not wrong his son Absalom, and so he asks for God's faithfulness and His promises to deliver those who believe in Him, so that He may deliver him from the hand of Absalom, who wants to kill him. This does not mean that David trusts in the perfection of his righteousness, or that he cannot bear that God should judge him, because it would reveal his weakness and sins, but he means that he did not sin against Absalom or the people, that they should rise against him and kill him.

143.0.2.en: 2- David asks God to deal with him by His righteousness and faithfulness, but at the same time he is a sinner and cannot bear that God should judge him. The solution is Christ the Savior, in whom divine justice is fulfilled on the Cross, and by His mercy He delivers David and every wronged person who believes in God, in the Old and New Testaments.

143.0.3.en: 3- The Litany of the Departed mentions that every person is a sinner even if his life on earth were one day; these words are taken from this psalm (v. 2).

143.1.0.en: For the enemy hath persecuted my soul; he hath smitten my life down to the ground; he hath made me to dwell in darkness, as those that have been long dead.

143.1.1.en: 1- It shows the cruelty of Absalom, who persecuted his father and crushed his soul with grief when he rose up against him and gathered the army to kill him, so that David became like one dead in the darkness of the tomb, as happened to Adam and Eve when they were driven out of Paradise; this is what Satan did to them, and this is the feeling of every sinful person who has not completed his repentance and returned to God, or the repentant person's view of the period of his fall before he repented.

143.1.2.en: 2- Christ bore the sufferings of the Cross and death for us, and Satan and all his followers among the wicked Jews persecuted Him, and humiliated Him by scourging and spitting, and all the sufferings of the Cross, until He died like one rejected, but He rose after this by the power of His divinity, to raise us up in Him.

143.1.3.en: 3- If Christ suffered all these sufferings for us, let us not be troubled if trouble befalls us, and God permits Satan to persecute us and humiliate us and make us fall into the darkness of sin, but with God's help we rise from sin, repent, and recover our spiritual zeal.

143.2.0.en: Therefore is my spirit overwhelmed within me; my heart within me is desolate. I remember the days of old; I meditate on all thy works;

143.2.1.en: I muse on the work of thy hands. I stretch forth my hands unto thee: my soul thirsteth after thee, as a thirsty land. Selah.

143.2.3.en: 1- David felt the weight of the trial upon him, until he was perplexed in finding a way out to deliverance, and here he returned to himself, and remembered God's works with him, and His works with His people, whom He delivered from the bondage of Egypt, brought out and sustained in the wilderness, and brought into the land of Canaan, which flows with milk and honey, so he thanked God and asked Him to deliver him, and even declared to Him his great need, and said that his soul had become like a dry land needing the divine water to water it; all this he said while stretching forth his hands in prayer.

143.2.4.en: 2- Here appears the importance of knowing the works of God and remembering them at all times, especially in trouble, for it is what restored David's peace, confirmed his faith, and gave him a fervent prayer that delivered him from his enemies.

143.2.5.en: 3- Stretching forth the hands does not mean only prayer, but also showing his need of God to quench his thirst, and it also means emptying himself of his own will, in addition to repentance and declaring complete inability to find a solution.

143.2.6.en: 4- These verses apply to Christ, whose spirit was wearied as a man, and whose heart was perplexed by the many pressures and sufferings, for how could He who had no sin become sin for us, and He expressed the sufferings of the Cross approaching Him, while in the Garden of Gethsemane, by saying, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me, and He stretched out His hands in fervent prayer, and His soul was in distress like a parched land, but He bore all this for our redemption.

143.2.7.en: 5- This passage ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for reflection on the works of God and for prayer to Him, that He may deliver us, satisfy us and strengthen us.

143.2.8.en: When you face any trouble, remember what Christ bore for your sake, and that by accepting the trouble you share in Christ's sufferings, and remember the works of God in the Holy Bible so that your faith increases and you keep your peace.

143.3.0.en: Hear me speedily, O LORD: my spirit faileth: hide not thy face from me, lest I be like unto them that go down into the pit.

143.3.1.en: The pit (al-jubb): a deep hole, and it is a type of Hades and hell.

143.3.2.en: 1- David calls to God, who is his only hope, and asks Him to hasten to his help and answer his request, because the trouble is severe and he cannot bear it, and his spirit is almost failing within him from the many threats and the intensity of grief. His asking God to hasten means his great need and his trust in God his deliverer.

143.3.3.en: 2- He also asks God to look upon him with His shining face, for if He does not look upon him he will be like those who go down into the pit and die. The pit is also a type of eternal torment, and this means David's declaration of his attachment and hope in God's care for him. He considers fellowship with God to be life, and if he loses this fellowship he dies.

143.4.0.en: Cause me to hear thy lovingkindness in the morning; for in thee do I trust: cause me to know the way wherein I should walk; for I lift up my soul unto thee.

143.4.2.en: 1- David begs God to pour out His mercies upon him, and would that this were soon, that is, in the early morning. The time of darkness has passed, which is the time of trouble that he likens to the darkness of the night, and he longs for the light of the morning. This is because he trusted in God, so his hope in God is firm and strong.

143.4.3.en: 2- David also asks God to make him know the way of deliverance from his trouble, and he declares to God that he has lifted up his soul to Him, so he seeks Him alone and does not rely on earthly things or on any man.

143.4.4.en: 3- The way that we need is Christ, and if we trust in Him, lift our hearts toward heaven and leave the lusts of the earth, it is easy for us to walk in the right faith in Christ our God.

143.5.0.en: Deliver me, O LORD, from mine enemies: I flee unto thee to hide me.

143.5.1.en: When the enemies threatened David he took refuge in God to be fortified in Him, and asked Him to deliver him from these threats, for he suffers from the evil of the wicked, but he believes that God is a strong fortress. And if David had fled from God by falling into sin, now that he has repented he takes refuge in Him, and God protects him from his enemies.

143.6.0.en: Teach me to do thy will; for thou art my God: thy spirit is good; lead me into the land of uprightness.

143.6.1.en: 1- David declares his allegiance and faith in God, for he says my God, so he is His follower, and he also seeks His good pleasure and will, and begs that God teach him how to please Him and do His will, because the word for good pleasure in Hebrew also means will. And learning how a person pleases God requires training and time. This means that David is ready to train and labor to please God his God. This shows his true love for God, and also his trust in the grace of God that will teach him.

143.6.2.en: 2- He describes the Holy Spirit of God as good, and this confirms his faith in the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and this is against the heresy of Macedonius, which appeared in the fourth century and was condemned at the Council of Constantinople in AD 381.

143.6.3.en: 3- He asks the Spirit of God to guide him and lead him to reach a level land, that is, an upright land in which there is no crookedness, meaning a life firm in God, and upright conduct by His commandments, and a level land free of dangers, that is, a life of peace in the hands of God. And after David's life on earth is completed he hopes for the land perfect in uprightness and truly level, which is the new earth, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven.

143.7.0.en: Quicken me, O LORD, for thy name's sake: for thy righteousness' sake bring my soul out of trouble. And of thy mercy cut off mine enemies, and destroy all them that afflict my soul: for I am thy servant.

143.7.1.en: 1- David concludes the psalm, asking God to bring him out of the trouble he suffers and to give him life, because he is almost dying from the pressure of the trouble upon him. His hope for life is built on his faith in God and His holy name, which is able to give him life, and it is exalted above all the pagan gods known in the Old Testament, because God alone is the giver of life by His Holy Spirit.

143.7.2.en: 2- David clings to God's righteousness, who promised to reward the righteous and punish the wicked, so David asks for God's righteousness and His promises to deliver him from his trouble, because he believes in Him and strives in the way of righteousness.

143.7.3.en: 3- God's mercy, mingled with His righteousness, is manifested, that is, His mercy on His children who walk by His commandments, such as David, in cutting off his enemies and destroying those who afflict his soul, because David is submissive to God and to His commandments, and he declares to God that he is His servant. God's righteousness destroys the wicked as a punishment for them, and at the same time it is a mercy to the righteous, confirming them in faith and making them grow in every good work.

143.7.4.en: 4- In Christ mercy and righteousness meet and are fulfilled, so these two verses are a prophecy about Christ, who bound Satan by His Cross, and at the same time gave salvation to those who believe in Him.

143.7.5.en: 5- God's grace to the righteous appears in God's mercy that cuts off and destroys the wicked, but it requires of a person that he declare his submission to God and to His commandments, so he says that he is the servant of God. Grace together with spiritual striving gives a person salvation.

143.7.6.en: 6- God's perfect mercy and perfect righteousness appear in eternity in the cutting off of the enemies and those who afflict the righteous, that is, He casts Satan and all his followers into eternal torment, and gives His righteous children everlasting joy in the Kingdom of Heaven.

143.7.7.en: Have a firm hope in God however much troubles rise against you, or you are wounded even in the house of your loved ones, for He is able to deliver you, keep you, comfort your heart and take away all your pains.

143.7.8.en: God delivers and blesses His people "Blessed be the LORD my rock, who teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight" v. 1 Introduction:

143.7.9.en: 1- Its author: the prophet David, as appears from the title of the psalm.

143.7.10.en: 2- When was it written? In the title of the psalm in the Septuagint translation there is "of David, against Goliath."

143.7.11.en: This means that it was written after his victory over Goliath. But in (v. 2) it mentions that God subdued his people under him, and this means that he had reigned over the children of Israel, and it mentions that God scattered his enemies (v. 6); from this it is concluded that David wrote the psalm after he became king and after his victories over the surrounding peoples, remembering his victory over Goliath.

143.7.12.en: 3- This psalm is a psalm of thanksgiving to God, who gives us victory over our enemies the demons, and gives us many good things, and cares for us throughout our lives.

143.7.13.en: 4- This psalm is a type of Christ, who triumphed over Satan, since David was a type of Christ.

143.7.14.en: 5- It appears here that God is the One working in His children, to give them victory over their enemies the demons?

143.7.15.en: 6- This psalm is classified as one of the psalms of battles, like Psalm 18, in which appears the power of God supporting His children.

143.7.16.en: 7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
